docs.title: Chapter 9: Benchmarks and Metrics
docs.text:
How fast is fast? The Iron Law of Chapter 1 gives the definition, but in practice processors are compared with a zoo of numbers: MIPS, FLOPS, Dhrystone, CoreMark, Embench, SPEC, LINPACK, STREAM, MLPerf. This chapter says what each one measures, how to turn it into a fair comparison, which kind of average to use, and how results get bent. The aim is that you can read a performance claim critically and write one honestly.

You should know the Iron Law and CPI (Chapter 1), and the cores of Chapter 8 give context for the embedded benchmarks. The memory system of Chapter 4 explains one of the pitfalls.

docs.title: 9.1 What "faster" means
docs.text:
Time is the only honest yardstick. Everything else is a stand-in for it.

\[\text{performance} = \frac{1}{\text{execution time}} \qquad\qquad X \text{ is } n \text{ times faster than } Y \iff n = \frac{\text{time}(Y)}{\text{time}(X)}\]

For example, if a program takes 15 s on machine Y and 10 s on X, then X is \(15/10 = 1.5\) times faster.

Two different questions need two different measures. How long does my one job take? is latency. How many jobs does the machine finish per hour? is throughput. A laptop user cares about the first; a web server about the second. Every number in this chapter is either a time or a rate derived from one.

docs.title: 9.2 Rate metrics, and why they mislead
docs.text:
MIPS, millions of instructions per second, is the instruction count divided by (time × \(10^6\)). It is easy to quote, but an instruction on one ISA does different work from an instruction on another, and even on one machine a program of many simple instructions scores a higher MIPS figure while finishing later.

FLOPS are floating-point operations per second (MFLOPS, GFLOPS, TFLOPS). They are meaningful for number crunching, when everyone counts operations the same way, on the same algorithm.

Example 9.1: higher MIPS, slower machine

Machine A runs a job as 2.0 billion simple instructions in 1.0 s: \(2.0\times10^9/10^6 = 2\,000\) MIPS. Machine B runs the same job as 1.2 billion richer instructions in 0.8 s: \(1.2\times10^9/(0.8\times10^6) = 1\,500\) MIPS.

B has the lower MIPS, and finishes \(1.0/0.8 = 1.25\) times sooner. MIPS rewarded A for doing more, smaller steps.

docs.title: 9.3 Synthetic benchmarks: Dhrystone
docs.text:
A synthetic benchmark is a small artificial program written to imitate the mix of operations in typical software, not a real application. It is small and portable, easy to compile for any processor, even one with no operating system. But "typical" is a guess, and a small program behaves unlike a large one.

Benchmark Year Exercises Reported as Whetstone 1972 Floating-point arithmetic and maths functions MWIPS Dhrystone 1984 Integer arithmetic, records, string copies and compares DMIPS

Dhrystone, by Reinhold Weicker, runs one loop over and over, and the raw result is Dhrystones per second. The VAX-11/780, marketed as a "1 MIPS" machine, scored 1 757 Dhrystones per second. So the score is divided by 1 757 and called DMIPS: "how many VAXes is this?". Dividing by the clock in MHz gives DMIPS/MHz, work per clock tick, a CPI-like figure that compares designs running at different clock rates.

Example 9.2: DMIPS

A core scores 351 400 Dhrystones per second at 100 MHz. $\(\frac{351\,400}{1\,757} = 200 \text{ DMIPS}, \qquad \frac{200\ \text{DMIPS}}{100\ \text{MHz}} = 2.0\ \text{DMIPS/MHz}\)$

Dhrystone is being retired, for three reasons.

  • It is tiny. Its code and data fit in any cache, so it never feels the memory wall.
  • It is compiler-sensitive. Clever compilers can remove or simplify parts of it, and much of the score comes from string copying, which some libraries hand-optimise for exactly this test.
  • It has no enforced rules. Vendors chose their own compiler, flags and libraries, so two "DMIPS" figures are rarely comparable.

Treat a DMIPS number as a rough hint only, and only when the compiler and flags are stated.

docs.title: 9.4 CoreMark and Embench
docs.text:
CoreMark (EEMBC, 2009) is a small, free benchmark for processor cores, designed to fix Dhrystone's flaws. It runs four kinds of work:

  • lists: find and sort in linked lists (pointer chasing);
  • matrices: multiply and add (loops and arithmetic);
  • a state machine: parse input (branchy and hard to predict);
  • CRC: a checksum of every result, so that nothing can be optimised away.

Its results are computed from data that the compiler cannot see in advance, and self-checked. The run rules are strict: run for at least 10 seconds, do not change the source, and report the compiler and flags with every score. The score is iterations per second, and CoreMark/MHz divides it by the clock.

Example 9.3: CoreMark scores

4 000 iterations in 10 s on a 100 MHz core gives a score of \(4\,000/10 = 400\) and \(400/100 = 4.0\) CoreMark/MHz.

How should CoreMark/MHz be read? These are rough orders of magnitude for one core, from published results; the exact figures depend on the compiler and flags, which is the point of reporting them.

Kind of core Rough CoreMark/MHz Why Tiny multicycle or bit-serial well below 1 Many cycles per instruction Simple in-order microcontroller about 2 to 4 Pipelined, about one instruction per cycle Superscalar in-order about 3 to 5 Sometimes two per cycle Wide out-of-order about 5 to 8 and more Many per cycle, good prediction

A design with a high CoreMark/MHz may reach only a low clock rate. The chip's real speed is CoreMark/MHz × MHz: the Iron Law again.

Other embedded benchmarks:

  • Embench is a free, open suite (2019) of about 20 real embedded programs. It reports speed relative to a reference core and code size, both as geometric means, because in embedded systems memory costs money.
  • CoreMark-PRO is EEMBC's bigger sibling: several integer and floating-point workloads with larger data, closer to real applications.
  • ULPMark is EEMBC's energy benchmark for microcontrollers: how much energy a standard task costs.

docs.title: 9.5 Big-system benchmarks
docs.text:
SPEC CPU 2017, from the Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation, consists of 43 benchmarks built from real applications: compilers, compression, physics, weather, chess and more. It has four suites, integer and floating point, each measured two ways.

  • SPECspeed: one copy of each program. How quickly does one job finish? (Latency.)
  • SPECrate: many copies at once. How much work per hour? (Throughput; it fills every core.)

Each result is a ratio against a fixed reference machine's time, and the overall score is the geometric mean of the ratios. Base results use the same conservative compiler flags for all programs; peak allows tuning per program. There are strict run and reporting rules, and published, reviewed results.

The specialists each measure one thing well.

Benchmark Measures Unit Used for LINPACK (HPL) Solving a huge dense system of linear equations FLOPS The TOP500 supercomputer list STREAM Sustained memory bandwidth: copy, scale, add and triad over big arrays GB/s The memory wall, the roofline (Chapter 5) MLPerf Training and inference of standard AI models Time to train, queries per second AI chips and systems Whole-device applications Browsing, photos, games Scores Phones and laptops

LINPACK rewards floating-point units and says little about a web server; STREAM ignores computation entirely.

Question Reach for How efficient is this small core, clock for clock? CoreMark/MHz, Embench How big will my embedded program be? Embench code size How fast is this server or desktop CPU on real code? SPEC CPU (speed or rate) How many floating-point operations can this machine sustain? LINPACK (HPL) Is my program limited by memory? STREAM, plus the roofline How good is this AI accelerator? MLPerf How fast is my application? Run your application: always the best benchmark

docs.title: Which mean?
docs.text:
For raw times of a fixed workload, the total (or the arithmetic mean) of the times is honest: it is how long the work takes. For results normalised to a reference machine, use the geometric mean: the \(n\)th root of the product of \(n\) ratios. It gives the same ranking whichever machine is chosen as the reference. The arithmetic mean of ratios does not.

Example 9.4: the arithmetic mean of ratios can contradict itself

Two machines X and Y run two programs. Times in seconds: X takes 1 s on program 1 and 10 s on program 2; Y takes 10 s and 1 s.

Reference X. Y's time ratios are \(10/1 = 10\) and \(1/10 = 0.1\). Their arithmetic mean is \((10 + 0.1)/2 = 5.05\), so Y looks about five times slower.

Reference Y. X's time ratios are \(1/10 = 0.1\) and \(10/1 = 10\). The arithmetic mean is again 5.05, so now X looks five times slower than Y.

Each machine is declared five times slower than the other. The geometric mean in either direction is \(\sqrt{10 \times 0.1} = 1\): the machines are equal on this workload, whichever is the reference.

docs.title: Faster is not everything: efficiency
docs.text:
• Performance per watt (CoreMark/mW, SPECrate per watt) decides battery life and data-centre electricity bills.
  • Energy per operation (picojoules per instruction). Energy is power × time, so a fast chip that finishes and sleeps can use less energy than a slow, frugal one.
  • Performance per area (CoreMark/mm²). Silicon costs money; this is how many cores fit on a die.

Example 9.5: speed against efficiency

Core X: 4.0 CoreMark/MHz at 1 000 MHz and 0.5 W gives \(4\,000\) CoreMark, and \(4\,000/0.5 = 8\,000\) CoreMark per watt. Core Y: 6.0 CoreMark/MHz at 2 000 MHz and 3 W gives \(12\,000\) CoreMark, and \(12\,000/3 = 4\,000\) CoreMark per watt.

Y is 3 times faster; X does twice the work per joule. Which is "better" depends on the product: a server or a watch.

docs.title: 9.7 Benchmarking honestly
docs.text:
Trap What happens Benchmark-specific tuning Compilers or libraries recognise a famous benchmark and special-case it Hidden flags The headline uses aggressive flags that your code will not Cherry-picking Only the tests you win are quoted Fits in cache A tiny benchmark never touches main memory, so it hides the memory wall Unequal systems More memory, a faster disk or a higher power limit on one side Peak against sustained A burst at turbo clock, before the chip heats up and slows down

A reporting checklist:

  1. State the exact workload and input size.
  2. State the system: core, clock (fixed or turbo), memory and cache sizes.
  3. State the software: compiler and version, every flag, the libraries.
  4. Repeat the runs; report the median and the spread; let caches and clocks warm up first.
  5. Use the right mean, and show the per-program results too.
  6. Make it reproducible: someone else should get the same number.

The best benchmark is the program you actually care about. Every other score is an estimate of it.

docs.title: 9.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Performance is 1 ÷ time. Rate metrics such as MIPS mislead across ISAs and programs; FLOPS only for like-for-like number crunching.
  • Dhrystone gives DMIPS (divide by 1 757) and DMIPS/MHz: historic, tiny and easily gamed. CoreMark fixes it with self-checking, run rules and CoreMark/MHz; Embench adds open, real programs and code size.
  • SPEC CPU 2017 uses real applications, speed and rate, and ratios against a reference; LINPACK, STREAM and MLPerf each measure one thing.
  • Use the geometric mean for normalised results, and compare efficiency per watt, per joule and per mm² as well as speed.
  • Report workload, system, compiler and flags, and repeat runs. The best benchmark is your own program.

docs.title: 9.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1. A core at 250 MHz scores 1 230 000 Dhrystones per second. What are its DMIPS and DMIPS/MHz?

Answer

\(1\,230\,000/1\,757 \approx 700\) DMIPS; \(700/250 = 2.8\) DMIPS/MHz.

Exercise 9.2. A CoreMark run completes 30 000 iterations in 15 s on a 500 MHz core. What are the score and CoreMark/MHz? Is the run valid?

Answer

Score \(= 30\,000/15 = 2\,000\); CoreMark/MHz \(= 2\,000/500 = 4.0\). The run lasted 15 s, at least the required 10 s, so the duration rule is met (the compiler and flags must still be reported).

Exercise 9.3. Why is a geometric mean used for SPEC's ratios?

Answer

The results are ratios against a reference machine. The geometric mean of ratios gives the same ranking whichever reference is chosen, whereas an arithmetic mean of ratios can flip, as Example 9.4 shows.

Exercise 9.4. Machine A takes 12 s on program 1 and 3 s on program 2; machine B takes 4 s and 9 s. Using A as the reference, compute B's time ratios and their arithmetic and geometric means. Repeat with B as the reference. What do you observe?

Answer

Reference A: B's ratios are \(4/12 = 0.333\) and \(9/3 = 3\). Arithmetic mean \(= (0.333 + 3)/2 = 1.667\); geometric mean \(= \sqrt{0.333 \times 3} = \sqrt{1} = 1\).

Reference B: A's ratios are \(12/4 = 3\) and \(3/9 = 0.333\). Arithmetic mean \(= 1.667\) again; geometric mean \(= 1\).

The arithmetic mean says each machine is 1.67 times slower than the other, a contradiction; the geometric mean says they are equal in both directions, as they are (total time is 15 s for A and 13 s for B, so with raw times B is slightly ahead).

Exercise 9.5. Core P: 3.0 CoreMark/MHz at 500 MHz, 0.2 W. Core Q: 5.0 CoreMark/MHz at 1 500 MHz, 2.5 W. Find the speed and CoreMark per watt of each, and say which suits a wearable device and which a server.

Answer

P: \(3.0 \times 500 = 1\,500\) CoreMark; \(1\,500/0.2 = 7\,500\) per watt. Q: \(5.0 \times 1\,500 = 7\,500\) CoreMark; \(7\,500/2.5 = 3\,000\) per watt. Q is 5 times faster; P does \(7\,500/3\,000 = 2.5\) times the work per joule. P suits a wearable device (battery life), Q a server (speed, within a power budget).

Exercise 9.6. Why is Dhrystone "tiny" a problem for comparing processors with different caches and memory systems?

Answer

Its code and data fit in any cache, so every processor runs it entirely out of the L1 cache and none of them experiences its memory wall. Two processors with very different memory systems can therefore post similar scores while performing very differently on real programs.

Exercise 9.7 (practical). Obtain the free CoreMark benchmark from EEMBC, build it with make (which runs it and writes run1.log and run2.log), and record the score, the compiler and flags printed in the log, and your CPU's base clock. Compute CoreMark/MHz. Rebuild with at least two optimisation levels (for example -O0 and -O3), three runs each. Pool results from your group's machines into a table with a geometric mean normalised to one reference machine.

Answer

A valid run lasts at least 10 s; CoreMark says so in its log if it did not. -O0 is typically several times slower than -O2 or -O3 on the same machine: the compiler is part of the result. Your geometric-mean ranking should not change when you pick a different reference machine; an arithmetic mean of ratios might.

Exercise 9.8. Your CoreMark score went up 40% between two runs. Before believing it, what three things do you check?

Answer

That the compiler and flags were the same; that the machine's clock really was the same (turbo, power mode, temperature, other programs running); and that both runs were valid (at least 10 s) and repeated. A 40% jump from one run is more likely a difference in the set-up than a real improvement.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Caches and Virtual Memory
docs.text:
A processor core can retire several instructions per cycle, but a trip to DRAM costs hundreds of cycles. The entire memory hierarchy exists to hide that gap. This chapter takes the microarchitect's view of a single core's memory system: how a cache finds a block and where it may put one, why caches miss and what cures each kind of miss, how to judge a design with one formula (average memory access time), what happens on stores, which helpers keep an out-of-order core fed, and how virtual memory and the TLB fit in front of the cache. The next chapter takes up the problem that arises when many cores each have a cache: coherence and consistency.

You should already know the memory wall of Chapter 1; Chapter 3 helps for the sections on non-blocking caches.

docs.title: 4.1 Why caches work
docs.text:
A student writing an essay keeps the three books in use open on the desk, a dozen on the shelf behind, the city library across town, and the national warehouse for anything else. Nearly every look-up hits the desk.

A cache is a small, fast memory that keeps copies of recently used data close to the processor. If the data is there, it is a cache hit; if not, a cache miss, and the request goes one level down. Caches are invisible to programs: they never change an answer, only how long it takes.

Fast memory is small and costly, and big memory is slow and cheap, so memories are stacked: the top is fast, the bottom is big.

Level Typical size Typical access time Registers about 100 B under 1 cycle L1 cache 32 to 64 KB about 4 cycles L2 cache about 1 MB about 12 cycles L3 cache 8 to 64 MB about 40 cycles DRAM gigabytes about 200 or more cycles SSD terabytes about 100 000 cycles Figure 4.1. Typical access times of the levels of the memory hierarchy, on a logarithmic scale. The figures are orders of magnitude for orientation.

It works because real programs show locality.

  • Temporal locality: something used now will probably be used again soon (a loop counter, the top of the stack, a popular variable). So keep recently used data.
  • Spatial locality: if address \(A\) is used, addresses near \(A\) probably will be too (walking through an array, running instructions in sequence). So fetch a whole neighbourhood at once.

That neighbourhood is a cache line or block, the unit a cache moves and stores. Today it is typically 64 bytes.

docs.title: 4.2 How a cache finds things
docs.text:
Every address is cut into three pieces that tell the cache where to look and what to check.

  • The offset picks the byte within a block. A 64-byte block needs 6 offset bits.
  • The index picks which set of the cache to look in.
  • The tag is the rest of the address. It is stored with the block and compared, to tell which of the many possible blocks is actually there.
Figure 4.2. An address split for a 32 KiB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines: 6 offset bits, 6 index bits and a 20-bit tag in a 32-bit address.

docs.title: Where may a block live?
docs.text:
• Direct-mapped: each block has exactly one possible place. It is simple and fast, but two blocks wanting the same place keep evicting each other.
  • Set-associative: each block may go in any of \(N\) places in its set (2-way, 4-way, 8-way, ...). It is a good compromise and the usual choice.
  • Fully associative: a block may go anywhere. There are no collisions, but every tag must be checked on every access, so it is used only for tiny caches.

Car parking is the picture: an assigned bay (direct-mapped), any bay on your floor (set-associative), any bay in the building (fully associative). The number of sets is capacity divided by (block size × associativity). When a set is full, one block must be evicted; the usual rule is LRU, least recently used: evict the block that has been untouched the longest.

Example 4.1: simulating a tiny cache

A cache has 4 blocks of 4 bytes each. The byte addresses referenced are 0, 4, 16, 0, 20, 4, 32, 0. With 4-byte blocks, the block number of an address is the address divided by 4: 0, 1, 4, 0, 5, 1, 8, 0. The offset has 2 bits.

Direct-mapped (4 sets, so the index is the block number mod 4):

Access Address Block Set Result Why 1 0 0 0 miss compulsory 2 4 1 1 miss compulsory 3 16 4 0 miss compulsory; evicts block 0 4 0 0 0 miss conflict: block 4 evicted it 5 20 5 1 miss compulsory; evicts block 1 6 4 1 1 miss conflict: block 5 evicted it 7 32 8 0 miss compulsory; evicts block 0 8 0 0 0 miss conflict

Zero hits: 5 compulsory misses and 3 conflict misses (0 and 16 fight over set 0; 4 and 20 fight over set 1).

2-way set-associative (2 sets of 2 ways, LRU; the set is the block number mod 2). Set 0 sees blocks 0, 4, 0, 8, 0: miss, miss, hit, miss (it evicts block 4, the least recently used), hit. Set 1 sees blocks 1, 5, 1: miss, miss, hit. That is 3 hits (the second 0, the second 4, the last 0) and 5 compulsory misses.

Fully associative (one set of 4 ways, LRU). The five distinct blocks 0, 1, 4, 5, 8 each miss once, compulsory. When block 8 arrives the cache holds 0, 1, 4 and 5, and block 4 is the least recently used, so it is evicted. The result is again 3 hits and 5 misses, all compulsory.

A conflict miss is exactly a miss that a fully associative cache of the same size would have avoided: here, the three extra misses of the direct-mapped cache.

docs.title: Spatial locality in action
docs.text: Take an array of four 4-byte words at addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, read twice in a cache of 16 bytes. With 4-byte blocks (4 blocks) the first pass misses on every word and the second pass hits every time: 4 misses in 8 accesses. With 8-byte blocks (2 blocks) the first access to each block brings in its neighbour: access 0 misses, 4 hits, 8 misses, 12 hits, and the second pass hits entirely: 2 misses in 8 accesses. Spatial locality halves the misses.

docs.title: 4.3 Why misses happen
docs.text:
Every miss has one of three causes, and each has its own cure. (The classification is due to Mark Hill.)

Kind Cause Cure Compulsory (cold) The first touch of a block: it was never in the cache Bigger blocks; fetching ahead (prefetching) Capacity The program's working data simply does not fit A bigger cache Conflict Too many busy blocks map to the same set, though the cache has room elsewhere More associativity

Multicore adds a fourth C, coherence, treated in Chapter 5: a block is invalidated because another core wrote it.

Two experiments make the difference concrete. In a direct-mapped cache of 4 blocks of 4 bytes, addresses 0 and 16 fall into the same set (blocks 0 and 4, both set 0), so alternating between them misses on every access. Switch to 2-way and, after the first two misses, every access hits. Now cycle through five blocks (addresses 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, repeatedly) in a four-block cache with LRU. Even a fully associative cache misses every time, because each block is evicted just before it is needed again; only a bigger cache helps. That is a capacity problem, not a conflict problem.

Every knob has a price.

Turn up... Compulsory Capacity Conflict Price Cache size none fewer fewer Slower hits, more area and power Associativity none none many fewer Slower hits (more tags to compare) Block size fewer can rise can rise Each miss fetches more bytes (higher miss penalty and bandwidth)

Block size has a sweet spot: too small wastes spatial locality, too big drags in bytes nobody uses and evicts useful ones. Sixty-four bytes is the near-universal choice. Associativity has diminishing returns, summarised in a rule of thumb: a direct-mapped cache of size \(N\) misses about as often as a 2-way cache of size \(N/2\).

docs.title: 4.4 Average memory access time
docs.text:
One formula judges any cache design:

\[\text{AMAT} = \text{hit time} + \text{miss rate} \times \text{miss penalty}\]

Every term is a design knob. Lowering the hit time favours small, simple, low-associativity L1 caches; lowering the miss rate favours big, associative caches; lowering the miss penalty is what the deeper levels are for. The terms trade against one another, so no one can be optimised alone.

Example 4.2: one level

An L1 hit takes 1 cycle, the miss rate is 4%, and going to DRAM costs 200 cycles. $\(\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.04 \times 200 = 1 + 8 = 9 \text{ cycles}\)$ The 4% of accesses that miss cost eight times more than the 96% that hit. Shrinking the penalty is what further levels are for.

With several levels the miss penalty of one level is the AMAT of the next:

\[\text{AMAT} = h_{L1} + m_{L1}\bigl(h_{L2} + m_{L2}(h_{L3} + m_{L3} \cdot t_{\text{DRAM}})\bigr)\]

Example 4.3: three levels

L1: hit 1 cycle, miss rate 5%. L2: hit 12 cycles, miss rate 40%. L3: hit 40 cycles, miss rate 50%. DRAM: 200 cycles. Work from the inside out.

  • L3 level: \(40 + 0.50 \times 200 = 140\)
  • L2 level: \(12 + 0.40 \times 140 = 68\)
  • L1 level: \(1 + 0.05 \times 68 = 4.4\) cycles

That is 4.4 cycles instead of 9. The miss rates here are local: the misses at that level divided by the accesses reaching that level. A global miss rate divides by all accesses made by the CPU. Mixing the two is a classic mistake.

docs.title: How the levels are arranged
docs.text:
• Contents. L1 is almost always split into an instruction cache and a data cache, so that the fetch engine and the load/store unit never contend; L2 and L3 are unified, one pool shared by instructions and data.
  • Placement. Each core usually has private L1 and L2 caches, for low latency; all cores share the last-level cache, which is the capacity and coherence backstop for the whole socket.
  • Inclusion. An inclusive cache keeps a copy of everything in the level above (simpler bookkeeping: to know what any core caches, snoop only the last level), at the price of duplicated capacity. An exclusive cache keeps each block in one level only (more total capacity, at the price of more careful handling when blocks move between levels). A non-inclusive, non-exclusive (NINE) design makes no promise either way.

docs.title: 4.5 Writes, and other tricks
docs.text:
Stores need rules of their own.

  • Write-through: every store updates the cache and the next level. It is simple and always up to date, but generates a lot of traffic, and needs a write buffer so that the core does not stall.
  • Write-back: a store updates only the cache and marks the block dirty. It is written down only when evicted. There is far less traffic, and it is the norm for L1 data caches and below. It needs a dirty bit and a write-back path.
  • Write-allocate: on a store miss, fetch the block first (the usual partner of write-back).
  • No-write-allocate: on a store miss, write straight to the next level without caching (the usual partner of write-through; good for streaming stores).

Several helpers keep an out-of-order core fed.

  • The write (store) buffer is a small FIFO that holds retired stores, so the core need not wait for them to reach memory. Loads must look inside it (store-to-load forwarding), and its draining behaviour is central to the memory-consistency model of Chapter 5.
  • A victim cache is a tiny fully associative buffer for recently evicted blocks. It catches conflict misses in a low-associativity L1 cheaply, adding a bit of associativity for the hot sets.
  • Prefetching brings blocks in before they are demanded, attacking compulsory misses. Hardware prefetchers (next-line, stride and stream) detect patterns such as "every 64 bytes" and run ahead; software prefetch hints (for example x86 PREFETCHT0 or the RISC-V Zicbop instructions) are precise but need their distance tuned. Too eager a prefetcher pollutes the cache and wastes bandwidth.
  • Non-blocking (lock-up-free) caches keep serving hits while a miss is pending ("hit under miss") and track several outstanding misses ("miss under miss") with MSHRs, the miss status handling registers. Each MSHR records the pending block's address and which loads are waiting; when the fill returns, it wakes them. The number of MSHRs caps the memory-level parallelism, the essential partner of an out-of-order core's ability to have many loads in flight.

docs.title: 4.6 Virtual memory and the TLB
docs.text:
Every program believes it has the whole memory to itself. A translation step makes that true. With virtual memory, programs use virtual addresses and the hardware translates each one to a physical address in real memory. Translation works in chunks called pages, commonly 4 KiB. A page table in memory lists where each virtual page really lives. This gives isolation (programs cannot see each other), freedom of placement, and the ability to keep rarely used pages on disk. It is like flat numbers in two buildings: "Flat 1" exists in both, and the postal service knows which street each building is on.

A flat page table would be enormous, so architectures use a multi-level (radix) table: the virtual address is split into fields that index successive levels. RISC-V Sv39, for example, uses three 9-bit levels above a 12-bit page offset.

Figure 4.3. Sv39 translation: three 9-bit virtual page number fields index three levels of page table; the 12-bit page offset passes through unchanged.

A full walk is one memory read per level, three extra reads for every access, which is far too slow to do each time. The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small, fast, highly associative cache of recent translations (virtual page number to physical page number, plus permission bits). A TLB hit translates in about a cycle; a miss triggers a page-table walk, by a hardware walker or on some ISAs by software. TLBs are split for instructions and data, often have two levels, and are tagged with an address-space identifier (ASID) so that a context switch need not flush them.

docs.title: The VIPT trick
docs.text:
If the L1 cache must be looked up after translation (physically indexed, physically tagged, PIPT), the TLB sits on the critical path and slows every access. If it is indexed by the virtual address (VIVT) there are aliasing problems. The compromise is VIPT: virtually indexed, physically tagged. Use the untranslated page-offset bits to index the cache set in parallel with the TLB look-up, then compare the physical tag once translation completes. The overlap is free, provided that

\[\text{number of sets} \times \text{block size} \le \text{page size}\]

so that the index and offset bits come entirely from the page offset, which translation does not change. This constraint is one reason so many L1 caches are 32 KiB, 8-way, with 64-byte lines: \(32\ \text{KiB}/8 = 4\ \text{KiB}\), exactly one page, and the 6 index bits plus 6 offset bits of Figure 4.2 make exactly the 12-bit page offset.

docs.title: 4.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Caches exploit temporal and spatial locality; data moves in cache lines, typically 64 bytes.
  • An address splits into tag, index and offset. Direct-mapped, set-associative and fully associative caches trade speed against collisions; LRU picks the victim.
  • Misses are compulsory, capacity or conflict (and, with several cores, coherence). Size cuts capacity misses, associativity cuts conflict misses, bigger blocks cut compulsory misses up to a point.
  • \(\text{AMAT} = \text{hit time} + \text{miss rate} \times \text{miss penalty}\), applied level by level with local miss rates.
  • Write-back with write-allocate is the norm; write buffers, victim caches, prefetching and non-blocking caches with MSHRs keep an out-of-order core fed.
  • Virtual memory translates pages through multi-level tables; the TLB caches translations; VIPT overlaps translation with the cache index.

docs.title: 4.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1. An L1 cache has a hit time of 2 cycles, a miss rate of 10% and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. What is the AMAT?

Answer

\(2 + 0.10 \times 100 = 12\) cycles.

Exercise 4.2. Two blocks keep evicting each other in a direct-mapped cache that is mostly empty. Which kind of miss is this, and what fixes it?

Answer

Conflict misses. More associativity fixes them (2-way would do here).

Exercise 4.3. Take the addresses 0, 4, 16, 0, 20, 4, 32, 0 for a cache of 4 blocks of 4 bytes, but now with 8-byte blocks (the cache is then 2 blocks of 8 bytes: direct-mapped means 2 sets). Simulate the direct-mapped cache and count hits.

Answer

With 8-byte blocks, the block number is the address divided by 8: 0, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 4, 0. The index is the block number mod 2: 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, so every access falls in set 0.

Access Address Block Result 1 0 0 miss 2 4 0 hit (same 8-byte block) 3 16 2 miss, evicts block 0 4 0 0 miss, evicts block 2 5 20 2 miss, evicts block 0 6 4 0 miss, evicts block 2 7 32 4 miss, evicts block 0 8 0 0 miss

One hit in eight accesses. The larger block gave one spatial-locality hit but the cache has only two sets, so conflicts dominate; compare the zero hits of Example 4.1.

Exercise 4.4. A two-level cache has: L1 hit 1 cycle, miss rate 8%; L2 hit 10 cycles, local miss rate 25%; memory 150 cycles. Find the AMAT with and without the L2.

Answer

With the L2: \(1 + 0.08 \times (10 + 0.25 \times 150) = 1 + 0.08 \times 47.5 = 4.8\) cycles. Without it: \(1 + 0.08 \times 150 = 13\) cycles.

Exercise 4.5. A cache is 32 KiB, 8-way set-associative, with 64-byte blocks, and addresses are 32 bits. (a) How many sets does it have? (b) Split the address 0x00012345 into tag, index and offset. (c) Is the cache usable as VIPT with 4 KiB pages?

Answer

(a) \(32\,768/(64 \times 8) = 64\) sets, so 6 index bits; the offset has 6 bits and the tag has \(32 - 12 = 20\) bits.

(b) The offset is the low 6 bits. \(0x345 = 837\) and \(837 \bmod 64 = 5\), so the offset is 5. The index is the next 6 bits: \(\lfloor 837/64 \rfloor = 13\), so the index is 13. The tag is the address shifted right by 12: \(0x00012345 \gg 12 = 0x12\).

(c) Sets × block size \(= 64 \times 64 = 4096\) bytes = 4 KiB, which equals the page size, so the index and offset bits come entirely from the page offset: yes, it can be VIPT.

Exercise 4.6. Why is a 16 KiB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks also VIPT-friendly with 4 KiB pages, but a 64 KiB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks is not?

Answer

The number of sets times the block size is the cache size divided by the associativity. For 16 KiB, 4-way this is \(16/4 = 4\) KiB, which fits in one page. For 64 KiB, 4-way it is \(64/4 = 16\) KiB, so 2 index bits would lie above the page offset and would be changed by translation: the cache cannot be indexed before the TLB answers without aliasing problems.

Exercise 4.7. A cache is direct-mapped with 4 blocks of 4 bytes. Addresses 0 and 16 are accessed alternately: 0, 16, 0, 16, 0, 16. How many hits? How many with a 2-way cache of the same size?

Answer

Direct-mapped: blocks 0 and 4 both map to set 0, so each access evicts the other: 0 hits in 6 accesses. 2-way: the two blocks sit in the two ways of the same set; after the first two compulsory misses all four remaining accesses hit: 4 hits in 6.

Exercise 4.8. With Sv39 paging and no TLB hit, how many memory reads does one load need in total, assuming the page-table reads and the data read all go to memory? Why does the TLB matter?

Answer

Three reads to walk the three table levels plus one read for the data itself: four. With a TLB hit the translation takes about a cycle and the load needs only the data access (and perhaps a cache hit), so the TLB removes the three extra reads from nearly every access.

Exercise 4.9. State one benefit and one cost of doubling the block size of a cache.

Answer

Benefit: fewer compulsory misses on code and data with spatial locality, since each miss brings in more neighbouring bytes. Cost: each miss fetches more bytes (a higher miss penalty and more bandwidth), fewer blocks fit so conflict and capacity misses can rise, and false sharing between cores becomes more likely.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Coherence, Consistency and Scaling
docs.text:
Give every core its own cache and the copies of the same data can disagree. This chapter explains how hardware keeps them in agreement (cache coherence, and the MESI protocol in particular), and then takes up a separate and subtler question: in what order may one core observe another core's writes to different locations (memory consistency)? It closes with what happens when the core count grows so large that one shared memory becomes the bottleneck: NUMA, and the roofline picture of the memory wall.

You need the caches of Chapter 4, and the store buffer and speculation of Chapters 3 and 4 help for the section on consistency.

docs.title: 5.1 The problem: stale copies
docs.text:
Both cores have cached \(X = 5\). Core 0 writes 9 into its own cache. Core 1 still reads 5. Without a rule, the two cores silently disagree.

Cache coherence is the hardware guarantee that fixes this. Informally, in a coherent system, for a single memory location:

  1. A read by a core returns the value of the last write by that core, if no other core wrote in between (program order is respected for one core).
  2. A write by one core is eventually made visible to all the others.
  3. Writes to the same location are serialised: all cores observe them in the same order.

Coherence is about a single location. Ordering across different locations is consistency, the subject of Section 5.5.

docs.title: 5.2 Two ways to keep watch
docs.text:
Snooping. Every cache watches a shared bus or ring. A write is announced to all; each cache checks its tags and reacts, either by invalidating its copy or by updating it. It is simple and low-latency at small scale, but broadcast bandwidth does not scale beyond about a dozen cores. It is like shouting across an open-plan office.

Directory. A directory, often located at the last-level cache or at a block's "home node", records for each block which cores hold copies and in what state. Writes send messages point to point, only to the sharers. It scales to many cores and to several chips, at the cost of the directory's storage and an extra indirection delay. It is like a receptionist who knows exactly whom to phone.

Most protocols are invalidation protocols: to write, a core first makes every other copy invalid. The rule behind them is many readers, or one writer, never both.

docs.title: 5.3 The MESI protocol
docs.text:
MESI is the canonical invalidation protocol. Each cached block is in one of four states.

State Valid? Matches memory? May others hold it? Meaning Modified yes No: this cache owns the only up-to-date copy No The only valid copy; memory is stale. It must be written back before another core reads it Exclusive yes Yes (clean) No The sole cached copy, unmodified. It can be written silently, moving to M with no bus traffic Shared yes Yes Yes, possibly A read-only copy; a write needs the other sharers invalidated first Invalid no not applicable not applicable The block is absent or stale: a read or write here misses

The E state is MESI's improvement over the older MSI protocol. A load that finds no other sharer lands in E, so a later store upgrades to M for free, with no invalidation broadcast. That is the common case for private data.

The principal bus transactions are:

  • BusRd: a read request.
  • BusRdX (read for ownership, RFO): a read with intent to write, which invalidates all other copies.
  • BusUpgr: an invalidation of the other sharers, sent when the core already holds the block in S and wishes to write.
Figure 5.1. MESI transitions. Panel (a): the moves caused by this core's own loads and stores. Panel (b): the moves caused by what this cache snoops from other cores.

Example 5.1: three cores and one block

Three cores C0, C1 and C2, and one block X, all start Invalid. The operations, in order, are: C0 reads, C1 reads, C0 writes, C2 reads, C2 writes, C1 reads.

Operation C0 C1 C2 Bus message and what happens Memory up to date? start I I I yes C0 reads E I I BusRd; no other copy, so C0 gets E yes C1 reads S S I BusRd; C0 snoops, supplies the data and moves E to S yes C0 writes M I I BusUpgr; C1 moves S to I no C2 reads S I S BusRd; C0 (in M) writes back and supplies the data, M to S yes C2 writes I I M BusUpgr; C0 moves S to I no C1 reads I S S BusRd; C2 (in M) writes back, M to S yes

Memory is stale only after the two writes, until the next read forces the write-back. Had C0 been the only reader before its write, it would have held X in state E, and the write would have been silent: E moves to M with no bus message at all.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text: MOESI adds an Owned state: a dirty block can be shared while one cache stays responsible for the eventual write-back, so dirty data can be passed from cache to cache without first updating memory (used by AMD). MESIF adds a Forward state: one sharer is designated the single responder to a read request, avoiding redundant replies from several caches (used in Intel's QPI and UPI).

docs.title: 5.4 A trap: false sharing
docs.text: Coherence works on whole blocks (64 bytes), not on single variables. Suppose core 0 keeps updating variable A and core 1 keeps updating variable B, and A and B happen to sit in the same block. Every write by one core invalidates the other core's copy, and the block ping-pongs between them. No data is really shared, yet the cores slow each other down, sometimes by a factor of 10 or more. This is false sharing, and it is the fourth C of Chapter 4 in action. The remedy is to place variables that different cores write in separate blocks, by padding or alignment.

docs.title: 5.5 Memory consistency models
docs.text:
Coherence handles one location. Consistency defines the allowed orderings of accesses to different locations, as seen by other cores. It is the contract between hardware and the concurrent programmer.

Model The rule Used by Sequential consistency (SC) The result is as if all cores' operations ran in some single interleaving, each core's operations appearing in its own program order. Intuitive, but forbids many hardware optimisations No mainstream high-performance processor TSO (total store order) A load may overtake an earlier store to a different address (stores wait in a FIFO store buffer); nothing else reorders x86, SPARC Weak or relaxed Almost any independent pair of accesses may be reordered Arm, RISC-V (RVWMO), Power

The classic demonstration is the store-buffer litmus test, sometimes called Dekker's test. Two flags A and B both start at 0:

Core 0 Core 1 A = 1 B = 1 r0 = B r1 = A

Under sequential consistency at least one of r0 and r1 must be 1: whichever store reaches memory first is seen by the other core's load. But with store buffers (TSO), both stores can still be waiting in their buffers when the loads execute, so \(r0 = r1 = 0\) is possible.

Outcome \((r0, r1)\) Allowed under SC? Allowed under TSO? (0, 1) yes yes (1, 0) yes yes (1, 1) yes yes (0, 0) no yes

A fence (memory barrier) forces earlier memory operations to complete before later ones start. Putting a full fence between the store and the load on each core forbids \((0,0)\) under every model.

x86      MFENCE  (and LOCK-prefixed read-modify-write instructions are full barriers)
Arm      DMB     (also DSB, ISB; plus acquire/release loads and stores LDAR and STLR)
RISC-V   FENCE rw,rw   (plus .aq and .rl bits on atomic operations; FENCE.I for the instruction cache)

Programming languages wrap fences in "atomics" with named memory orders (in C11 and C++11: relaxed, acquire, release and sequentially consistent), which the compiler lowers to the right fences on each target. Programmers rarely write fences by hand, but locks and flags rely on them.

Coherence is not consistency

Coherence makes the caches agree about each individual location. Consistency governs the order seen across locations. A machine can be perfectly coherent and still let one core observe another's writes to X and Y out of order. Fences fix ordering; they do not "make the caches coherent", because they already are. You need both, and different mechanisms provide them.

docs.title: 5.6 Scaling up: NUMA and the roofline
docs.text:
As the core count grows, a single shared memory becomes the bottleneck, so big servers become NUMA (non-uniform memory access): each socket or chiplet owns part of the DRAM. Its own part is fast; another node's part is reached across an interconnect (Intel UPI, AMD Infinity Fabric) and is slower. Software must be NUMA-aware. A first-touch allocation policy places a page in the node of the thread that first writes it, and thread pinning keeps a thread near its data. Coherence at this scale is directory-based.

The roofline model draws the memory wall as a picture. Plot the attainable performance (operations per second) against the arithmetic intensity (operations per byte of DRAM traffic). Two ceilings form a roof: a slanted line on the left, where performance is intensity times memory bandwidth, and a flat line on the right at the peak compute rate. A kernel under the slanted part is memory-bound; to improve it, raise its intensity by reusing data (blocking), or raise the effective bandwidth with prefetching. A kernel under the flat part is compute-bound. The ridge point, where the two lines meet, is the intensity a kernel needs to stop being starved by the memory system.

Figure 5.2. A roofline sketch: a slanted bandwidth roof and a flat compute roof meet at the ridge point. Kernel A is memory-bound; kernel B is compute-bound.

docs.title: 5.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Coherence keeps the copies of one location in agreement: many readers or one writer. Snooping broadcasts; a directory records the sharers and scales.
  • MESI has four states (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid). The E state makes the write to private data silent. MOESI and MESIF add owned and forward states.
  • False sharing makes cores slow each other down when unrelated variables share a 64-byte block.
  • Consistency models (SC, TSO, weak) define the order of accesses to different locations. Fences restore order where it matters; atomics hide them in high-level code.
  • Coherence and consistency are different guarantees. NUMA and the roofline scale the ideas of caching and locality up to whole systems.

docs.title: 5.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1. Core 2 holds X in state M. Core 0 reads X. What happens?

Answer

Core 0's read misses and goes on the bus (BusRd). Core 2 snoops it, supplies the data and writes it back to memory. Both copies end up Shared (S).

Exercise 5.2. Trace the sequence C0 reads, C1 reads, C1 writes, C0 reads of one block X, with all caches initially Invalid. Give the state of each cache after each step.

Answer

C0 reads: C0 = E, C1 = I (BusRd, no other copy). C1 reads: C0 = S, C1 = S (BusRd; C0 supplies and moves E to S). C1 writes: C1 = M, C0 = I (BusUpgr invalidates C0's copy; memory is now stale). C0 reads: C1 writes back and supplies the data; C1 = S and C0 = S (memory is up to date again).

Exercise 5.3. Why is the Exclusive state valuable?

Answer

A core that reads a block nobody else holds gets it in E. If it later writes, E moves to M silently, with no bus transaction and no invalidation. In MSI such a block would arrive in S and the write would need an invalidation broadcast, so for private data (the common case) E saves a bus message per write.

Exercise 5.4. Two threads on two cores increment two different counters. The program runs ten times slower than the same two threads run one after the other. Name the likely cause and one fix.

Answer

False sharing: the two counters lie in the same 64-byte block, so every increment invalidates the other core's copy and the block ping-pongs. The fix is to put the counters in separate blocks, by padding each to at least 64 bytes or by aligning them to 64-byte boundaries.

Exercise 5.5. In the litmus test of Section 5.5, list every possible final value of \((r0, r1)\) under sequential consistency, and the extra one that TSO permits. What must be added to forbid it?

Answer

Under SC: (0,1), (1,0) and (1,1). TSO also permits (0,0), because both stores may still sit in store buffers when the loads execute. A full fence (MFENCE on x86, FENCE rw,rw on RISC-V) between the store and the load on each core forbids it.

Exercise 5.6. "Fences make the caches coherent." Is this true? Explain.

Answer

No. The caches are already kept coherent by the coherence protocol, whether or not any fence executes. A fence orders one core's accesses to different locations as seen by other cores; that is a consistency property.

Exercise 5.7. A kernel performs 2 operations for each byte it fetches from DRAM. The machine's ridge point is at 8 operations per byte. Is the kernel memory-bound or compute-bound? Name one change that would help.

Answer

Its intensity (2) is to the left of the ridge point (8), so it is memory-bound: it sits under the slanted roof. Raising the intensity by reusing data already fetched (blocking or tiling the computation), or raising the effective bandwidth with prefetching, would help; a faster arithmetic unit would not.

Exercise 5.8. What is a "first-touch" policy, and why does it help on a NUMA machine?

Answer

A page is placed in the memory of the node whose thread first writes it. If each thread initialises the data it will later use, that data lives in its own node's DRAM, where access is fast, instead of across the slower inter-node link.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: ACK / NACK In I²C, the acknowledgement (or its absence) that a receiver signals after each byte by pulling SDA low (ACK) or leaving it high (NACK). AMAT (average memory access time) Hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty; with several levels, the miss penalty of one level is the AMAT of the next. Amdahl's law If a fraction \(p\) of the work is sped up by a factor \(s\), the overall speed-up is \(1/((1-p) + p/s)\), which can never exceed \(1/(1-p)\). AXI Arm's Advanced eXtensible Interface: five independent VALID/READY channels (AW, W, B, AR, R) with bursts and outstanding, reorderable transactions. Back-pressure A receiver slowing a sender by keeping READY low; the sender holds its data and waits. Baud rate The number of bits per second on a serial line; both ends of a UART must be set to the same value. BOOM The Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine: a parameterisable superscalar out-of-order RISC-V core written in Chisel. Branch target buffer (BTB) A small table, indexed by a branch's address, that remembers where the branch jumped last time, so fetch can redirect immediately. Bubble An empty slot that travels down a pipeline in place of an instruction that was stalled. Burst A run of data beats described by a single address beat. Cache A small, fast memory that keeps copies of recently used data close to the processor. Cache line (block) The unit of data a cache stores and moves; typically 64 bytes. Chipyard Berkeley's framework that composes Rocket, BOOM, caches, TileLink and peripherals into complete SoCs. Common data bus (CDB) In Tomasulo's algorithm, the bus on which a finished unit broadcasts (tag, value) so that all waiting instructions can capture it. Constant-time code Code whose running time, memory addresses and control flow do not depend on secret data. Coherence The guarantee that all caches agree about the value of each individual memory location. Consistency model The rules for the order in which accesses to different locations may be observed by other cores. CPI / IPC Cycles per instruction, and its reciprocal, instructions per cycle. CPOL / CPHA The two SPI settings that fix the idle level of the clock and the edge on which data is sampled. Crossbar A full switch connecting every manager to every subordinate, so that non-conflicting transfers proceed in parallel. Dennard scaling The long-lived trend in which smaller transistors also needed less voltage, keeping power per unit area constant; it ended around 2005. DMA (direct memory access) A hardware engine that copies blocks of data between memory and devices without CPU involvement for each word. Directory A record, per cache block, of which cores hold copies; used for coherence at larger scale. DLP / ILP / TLP Data-level, instruction-level and thread-level parallelism. Flit A flow-control unit: the fixed-size piece of a packet that moves through a network-on-chip. Forwarding (bypassing) Wires that carry a result straight from a pipeline register into a later instruction's ALU input, skipping the register file. False sharing Slowdown caused by unrelated variables that happen to share a cache block, so that writes by different cores invalidate each other's copies. Fence (memory barrier) An instruction that forces earlier memory operations to complete before later ones begin. GPIO A general-purpose input/output pin that software can drive or read. Hazard Anything that stops the next instruction from proceeding in its planned cycle: structural, data or control. Hysteresis Resistance to change: in a 2-bit branch predictor, the need for two successive surprises before the prediction flips. I²C A two-wire (SDA and SCL), open-drain, multi-device serial bus with addresses and per-byte acknowledgement. Instruction window The pool of decoded instructions from which an out-of-order core may choose what to execute. Interconnect The fabric of buses, crossbars or networks that lets the blocks of a chip communicate. ISA (instruction set architecture) The contract between software and hardware: registers, instructions, memory model, exceptions. Iron Law CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock period. Latency / throughput The time for one operation to complete, and the number of operations completed per unit time. Load-use hazard A load followed immediately by an instruction that uses the loaded value; costs one stall even with forwarding. Load/store queue (LSQ) The structure that holds in-flight memory operations in order, performing store-to-load forwarding and memory disambiguation. Manager / subordinate The block that starts a bus transaction, and the block that answers it (formerly master and slave). Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) Device registers placed in the address space so that ordinary loads and stores reach them. Memory wall The growing gap between processor speed and DRAM latency. MESI The four-state invalidation coherence protocol: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid. Microarchitecture The implementation of an ISA: pipeline, caches, predictors, execution units. MIPS Millions of instructions per second; a misleading performance metric. MSHR Miss status handling register: tracks one outstanding cache miss in a non-blocking cache. Network-on-chip (NoC) A packet-switched network of routers and links inside a chip. NUMA Non-uniform memory access: memory whose access time depends on which node owns it. Open-drain An output that can only pull a line low; a pull-up resistor supplies the high level. Out-of-order execution Starting instructions in any order that respects their dependences, while committing them in program order. Pipeline A datapath divided into stages so that several instructions are in progress at once. Precise exception An exception for which every earlier instruction has completed and no later instruction has changed any state. Prefetching Fetching data into the cache before it is demanded. RAW / WAR / WAW Read after write (a true dependence), write after read and write after write (false, name dependences). Register renaming Mapping architectural registers onto a larger physical register file so that every write gets a fresh register. Reorder buffer (ROB) A queue of all in-flight instructions in program order; instructions commit from its head. Reservation station A buffer in front of a functional unit in which an instruction waits for its operands. Roofline model A plot of attainable performance against arithmetic intensity, bounded by a bandwidth roof and a compute roof. RV64GC The RISC-V base 64-bit integer ISA with the M, A, F, D and C extensions: the usual baseline for a Linux-class core. Scoreboard The central bookkeeping structure of the CDC 6600 that tracked units and registers for out-of-order execution. Side channel A leak of secret information through unintended signals such as time, power or cache state. SMT (simultaneous multithreading) Issuing instructions from several threads into the same execution units in the same cycle. SPI Serial peripheral interface: a four-wire, clocked, full-duplex bus with a chip-select line per device. Speculation Executing instructions down a predicted path before the branch or fault that governs them is resolved. Superscalar A core that fetches, issues and commits several instructions per cycle. TileLink An open interconnect protocol from SiFive that scales from simple registers to full cache coherence. TLB (translation lookaside buffer) A small cache of recent virtual-to-physical page translations. Tomasulo's algorithm Dynamic scheduling with reservation stations, tag-based renaming and a common data bus. Transient execution Execution of wrong-path instructions that is later squashed; its architectural effects are undone but its cache footprint remains. UART Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter: a two-wire serial link with no shared clock. VALID/READY The handshake in which a transfer happens only when the sender's VALID and the receiver's READY are both high. VIPT Virtually indexed, physically tagged cache: the index comes from untranslated address bits, the tag from the translated address. VLIW Very long instruction word: an architecture in which the compiler packs independent operations into one wide instruction.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
The following are standard references for the subjects of this book, and the places where the tools it mentions are documented. Check publication details and current versions before citing.

Textbooks

  • John L. Hennessy and David A. Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. The standard graduate text on pipelining, instruction-level parallelism, memory hierarchy and multiprocessors.
  • David A. Patterson and John L. Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface, RISC-V edition. A gentler introduction that builds a RISC-V processor, pipeline and memory system.

Original sources named in the text

  • R. M. Tomasulo, "An efficient algorithm for exploiting multiple arithmetic units", IBM Journal of Research and Development, 1967, the paper behind reservation stations and the common data bus.
  • J. E. Smith and A. R. Pleszkun, work on implementing precise interrupts in pipelined processors (1988), the origin of the reorder buffer.
  • The Spectre and Meltdown papers of 2018, by their respective research teams, which introduced the transient-execution attacks of Chapter 10.

Specifications and projects

  • The RISC-V unprivileged and privileged specifications, published by RISC-V International.
  • Arm's AMBA specifications (APB, AHB, AXI, CHI) and the TileLink specification from SiFive.
  • The open-source projects of Chapters 8 and 11: Ripes (github.com/mortbopet/Ripes), gem5 (github.com/gem5/gem5), Chipyard (github.com/ucb-bar/chipyard), rocket-chip, BOOM, Verilator, GTKWave, Spike (github.com/riscv-software-src/riscv-isa-sim), PicoRV32 (github.com/YosysHQ/picorv32) and EEMBC's CoreMark.
  • The SPEC CPU 2017 documentation, the Embench suite, and the STREAM, LINPACK and MLPerf pages, for the rules and reporting formats of the benchmarks of Chapter 9.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Labs and a Design Study
docs.text:
Reading about pipelines, out-of-order execution and caches gets you halfway. The other half is watching them run. Every tool in this chapter is free and open-source and can be installed on a laptop. You start with a pipeline that you can single-step, move down to a cycle-level simulator that models a real out-of-order core, then generate and simulate an actual RISC-V system-on-chip, and finally look at the individual wires of a tiny core. Nothing here needs an FPGA or a fabrication run, only a terminal. The chapter ends with a measured design study in which you answer one microarchitecture question with evidence.

The four labs are ordered by depth. Do them in order the first time. Before every run, write down what you expect. A measurement teaches you something only when it can surprise you.

A word on commands

The commands in this chapter are those of the tools' own instructions at the time of writing. Class and option names change between releases (the names of Chipyard configurations and of gem5 statistics in particular), so check each project's current documentation, and search the configuration folder or stats.txt for the nearest match when a name is not found. On Windows, run the labs of this chapter, except the first, inside WSL2, not in the native command prompt or PowerShell: the toolchains assume a POSIX environment. Builds are large; do not cancel a compile that "looks stuck".

docs.title: 11.1 The ladder of tools

docs.title: 11.2 Lab 1: Ripes, a pipeline that moves one clock at a time
docs.text:
Ripes is a free graphical RISC-V simulator. It animates the datapath cycle by cycle: instructions slide through fetch, decode, execute, memory and write back; forwarding paths light up; hazards insert bubbles; and a cache model shows hits and misses. It models single-cycle and five-stage in-order processors, with or without forwarding and hazard detection, a branch model, and a parametrisable L1 cache (size, associativity, replacement and write policy). It is in-order only: for out-of-order behaviour you need gem5.

Getting it. Ripes ships as one prebuilt binary for Windows, macOS and Linux, so no compiler is needed to start: fetch a ready-made release from the project's page (github.com/mortbopet/Ripes, under Releases). On Linux it is an AppImage. It can also be built from source, which needs Qt 6, CMake and a C++17 compiler.

The program: add up an array. Open the Editor tab, paste the program below, then in the Processor tab choose the five-stage processor with forwarding and hazard detection, and step one clock at a time. The loop is a classic source of a load-use hazard and a taken branch on each iteration.

.data
arr:    .word 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6
        .text
        .globl  main
main:   la      a0, arr         # a0 = address of arr[0]
        li      a1, 8           # a1 = count
        li      a2, 0           # a2 = running sum
loop:   lw      t0, 0(a0)       # load arr[i]
        add     a2, a2, t0      # use it at once: a load-use hazard
        addi    a0, a0, 4       # next element
        addi    a1, a1, -1      # one fewer to go
        bnez    a1, loop        # back if not done: a control hazard
end:    j       end

Predict first. What will a2 hold at the end? Where will a bubble appear on every pass? What happens after each taken bnez? The answers: \(a2 = 3+1+4+1+5+9+2+6 = 31\); one bubble between lw and add; and the wrongly fetched instructions after a taken branch are flushed.

As you step, watch three things in the datapath view.

  1. Forwarding paths. After lw t0, the add depends on t0. With forwarding on, a wire from a later stage lights up and feeds the value to the ALU input.
  2. The load-use bubble. A load's result is not ready until MEM, so even with forwarding the dependent add stalls exactly one cycle, and you see a bubble injected.
  3. The branch. bnez resolves late, so a taken branch flushes the wrongly fetched instructions. The cycle counter and the pipeline diagram update live.

Example 11.1: predicting the cycle count by hand

Make the assumptions explicit: five stages with full forwarding; the branch is resolved in EX; the front end always fetches the next instruction in line (predict not taken), so a taken branch flushes two instructions and costs 2 cycles. Count only the eight passes of the loop and ignore the set-up instructions and the fill and drain.

  • Each pass has 5 instructions: lw, add, addi, addi, bnez.
  • add uses t0 straight after lw: 1 load-use stall per pass.
  • The first seven passes end in a taken branch: 2 more cycles each. The eighth falls through: no penalty.

Passes 1 to 7 take \(5 + 1 + 2 = 8\) cycles each, and pass 8 takes \(5 + 1 = 6\): a total of \(7 \times 8 + 6 = 62\) cycles for 40 instructions, a CPI of \(62/40 = 1.55\).

Now move addi a0,a0,4 between lw and add. The add is then two instructions behind the lw, and gets t0 by forwarding with no stall. A pass takes \(5 + 2 = 7\) cycles when the branch is taken and 5 when it is not: \(7 \times 7 + 5 = 54\) cycles, a CPI of \(54/40 = 1.35\). Scheduling the code by hand saved one cycle per pass: 8 cycles in all.

Ripes will report different absolute numbers (its own model of the branch, the set-up instructions, the fill and drain), but the differences between the configurations should have the same shape.

Suggested experiments.

Experiment Do this Expect to see Forwarding on or off Run on the model without forwarding and note the cycles; then with forwarding Without it each dependence stalls up to 2 cycles; with it only the load-use pair stalls, for 1 Kill the bubble Move addi a0,a0,4 between the lw and the add The bubble disappears: you scheduled the code by hand Cache Enable the data cache, then shrink it or change its associativity First-touch misses, then hits; a direct-mapped cache conflicts sooner than a 2-way one Longer loop Grow the array to 64 or more words The CPI settles above 1.0; the gap is the hazard penalty of Chapter 2

docs.title: 11.3 Lab 2: gem5, measuring a real out-of-order core
docs.text:
gem5 is the research-grade, cycle-level simulator used throughout academia and industry. Where Ripes shows one in-order pipeline, gem5 models complete systems and, crucially, a real out-of-order core, so that you can measure the effects of Chapters 3 and 4. It offers CPU models along a speed and detail scale:

  • AtomicSimple: the fastest, functional, no timing;
  • TimingSimple: in order, with real memory timing;
  • Minor: an in-order pipeline;
  • O3: out of order, with a reorder buffer, issue queue, load/store queue, renaming and speculation.

It also models a configurable memory hierarchy (levels, associativity, replacement), buses and crossbars, branch predictors and DRAM controllers. You configure the machine in a Python script and gem5 runs your binary on it.

Building it (Ubuntu or Debian, or WSL2): a C++ toolchain, SCons and a few libraries, then the build of the RISC-V variant. The first build is long.

sudo apt install build-essential scons python3-dev git m4 zlib1g-dev \
                 libprotobuf-dev protobuf-compiler libboost-all-dev
git clone https://github.com/gem5/gem5.git
cd gem5
scons build/RISCV/gem5.opt -j$(nproc)    # long the first time: be patient

Running a program on the out-of-order core. In "syscall emulation" mode gem5 runs a statically linked user program directly, with no operating system. The shipped configuration script wires up a CPU, caches and memory from command-line switches.

# a small static RISC-V program
riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc -O2 -static hello.c -o hello

build/RISCV/gem5.opt configs/deprecated/example/se.py \
    --cmd=hello --cpu-type=O3CPU \
    --caches --l2cache \
    --l1d_size=32kB --l1i_size=32kB --l1d_assoc=8 \
    --l2_size=256kB --l2_assoc=8

grep ipc m5out/stats.txt                          # instructions per cycle
grep "dcache.overallMissRate" m5out/stats.txt
grep -iE "branchPred.*(mispred|lookups)" m5out/stats.txt

The results land in m5out/, and the numbers are in stats.txt as name-and-value pairs. Names differ slightly across gem5 versions; if a grep finds nothing, open stats.txt and search for the closest match. As a sanity check, on O3 well-behaved code should show an IPC above 1.0, while on TimingSimple the IPC can never exceed 1.0. If your O3 run looks like an in-order core, you left --cpu-type at its default: always pass it explicitly.

Experiment Change Compare Cache size sweep --l2_size = 64kB, 256kB, 1MB L2 miss rate and IPC: diminishing returns, the memory wall as a graph Associativity --l1d_assoc = 1, 2, 8 Conflict misses fall as associativity rises In order against out of order TimingSimpleCPU against O3CPU IPC and cycles: how much latency out-of-order execution hides Branch cost A branch-heavy program Mispredictions × flush penalty ≈ lost cycles

Copy m5out/ aside after each run: the next run overwrites it.

docs.title: 11.4 Lab 3: Chipyard, a real SoC from Rocket and BOOM
docs.text:
Chipyard is Berkeley's open framework for building RISC-V systems-on-chip. It bundles generators (rocket-chip with the in-order Rocket core, BOOM, caches, the TileLink interconnect, peripherals and more), all written in Chisel and elaborated to synthesisable Verilog. Unlike gem5, a C++ model, Chipyard produces the actual hardware description that you could push through a physical-design flow to a real chip. This is where Chapters 6 and 8 become tangible.

A configuration is a Scala class that composes generators into an SoC. RocketConfig gives an in-order Rocket tile; a large BOOM configuration (for example LargeBoomV3Config, whose name varies by release) gives a wide out-of-order BOOM tile. Both attach L1 caches to an L2 and system memory over a TileLink fabric, with UART, GPIO and SPI peripherals on a peripheral bus. You then simulate the generated Verilog with Verilator.

Setting up. Chipyard is heavy: it pulls a large RISC-V toolchain and many Chisel dependencies through a one-time setup script. It needs Linux or WSL2, plenty of disk and time.

git clone https://github.com/ucb-bar/chipyard.git
cd chipyard
./build-setup.sh riscv-tools    # once: toolchain and dependencies (long)
source env.sh                   # in every new terminal

One program, two microarchitectures. Simulation lives under sims/; the Verilator flow is in sims/verilator, and the CONFIG make variable selects the SoC. The first build elaborates Chisel into Verilog and compiles the simulator, which is slow; later runs reuse it.

cd sims/verilator
make CONFIG=RocketConfig                   # build the simulator (slow once)
make CONFIG=RocketConfig run-binary \
     BINARY=$RISCV/riscv64-unknown-elf/share/riscv-tests/isa/rv64ui-p-add

make CONFIG=LargeBoomV3Config run-binary \
     BINARY=$RISCV/riscv64-unknown-elf/share/riscv-tests/isa/rv64ui-p-add

Changing the microarchitecture is a one-line change of configuration: BOOM shares the same TileLink and peripheral scaffolding, so only the tile changes. Compare the cycle counts of the two runs: same ISA, same binary, different microarchitecture. (A tiny single-instruction test mostly measures start-up, so for a more telling comparison run a longer program such as a benchmark.)

Where TileLink shows up. After elaboration, look under generated-src/ for the Verilog. Modules such as TLXbar and TLBuffer are the TileLink crossbar and pipeline registers, and the system, memory and peripheral buses wire the tile to the L2 cache, DRAM and the UART and GPIO. This is the interconnect chapter rendered as real, synthesisable modules: you can open the Verilog and trace a load from the core to memory through the crossbar.

docs.title: 11.5 Lab 4: Verilator and GTKWave, down to the wires
docs.text:
To really see a core work you simulate its hardware description and stare at the signals. Verilator compiles synthesisable Verilog into a fast C++ model; you drive it with a small test bench, dump a waveform file (VCD), and open it in GTKWave. The core to use is PicoRV32, the tiny, size-optimised, in-order core of Chapter 8, which is a single readable Verilog file, so nothing is hidden.

sudo apt install verilator gtkwave
git clone https://github.com/YosysHQ/picorv32.git
cd picorv32
make test_verilator       # build the model and run its test firmware
gtkwave testbench.vcd     # open the recorded waveform

If your checkout gates tracing behind a flag, enable it explicitly (for example --trace among the Verilator flags). If you write your own harness, recording a waveform always takes the same few lines: open a trace, then dump it every half clock.

Verilated::traceEverOn(true);
VerilatedVcdC* tfp = new VerilatedVcdC;
top->trace(tfp, 99);  tfp->open("testbench.vcd");
// each half clock:  top->clk = !top->clk; top->eval(); tfp->dump(t++);
tfp->close();

What to look for. Add clk, resetn and the memory interface: mem_valid, mem_ready, mem_addr, mem_wdata and mem_rdata, and the program counter. You will watch instruction fetches march through memory, see the valid and ready pair gate every access (the same handshake idea as AXI in Chapter 6) and confirm the reset behaviour. Zoom into one memory transaction and follow it from request to answer. If the waveform file is empty, tracing was not switched on: add --trace to Verilator or the traceEverOn and dump lines to your harness.

docs.title: 11.7 Capstone: measure one design decision
docs.text:
Choose one change, implement it, and quantify the effect with a before-and-after number.

  • A. A prefetcher. In gem5, enable a stride prefetcher on a loop that walks memory, and measure the change in miss rate and IPC.
  • B. A wider core. In Chipyard, move from a small to a large BOOM configuration and compare cycles on the same binary (and CoreMark if you can). Where do the extra resources stop helping?
  • C. Associativity. In gem5, vary the L1 associativity (1, 2, 4, 8) at a fixed size: where do conflict misses stop mattering?
  • D. A new device. In Chipyard, attach a simple memory-mapped register device to the peripheral bus, write a bare-metal program that pokes its registers, and find the TileLink transaction in a waveform.

In every case state a hypothesis first, run the baseline, run the variant, and report the difference as a number. That before-and-after number is the whole point of a microarchitecture lab.

docs.title: How to write it up
docs.text:
Every experiment report should contain:

  1. the question and your prediction;
  2. the set-up: machine, clock, operating system, tool and compiler versions, flags;
  3. a table of results, with at least 3 runs of each and the median reported;
  4. one chart;
  5. what matched your prediction, what did not, and why.

The design study is two pages: question, hypothesis, set-up, baseline, variant, the difference (with its spread over runs) and what you would try next. A marking guide that rewards the right things is: a clear question and prediction (15%); a reproducible set-up (20%); correct measurements, repeated (30%); honest interpretation (25%); presentation (10%).

docs.title: 11.8 Summary
docs.text:
• Ripes makes the five-stage pipeline, forwarding and hazards visible; predict the cycle count by hand first.
  • gem5 is cycle-level: run a binary on the out-of-order O3 core and read the IPC, cache miss rates and branch mispredictions from stats.txt, sweeping cache size and associativity and comparing in-order with out-of-order. Always pass --cpu-type explicitly.
  • Chipyard generates real synthesisable Rocket and BOOM SoCs wired over TileLink, simulated with Verilator.
  • Verilator and GTKWave take you to the waveform of a tiny core such as PicoRV32. Spike is the golden functional check.
  • The capstone is simple: change one thing and measure the difference. Report the set-up honestly and repeat the runs.

docs.title: 11.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 11.1. You run the same binary on gem5's TimingSimple and O3 models and both report an IPC of 0.8. What is the likely mistake?

Answer

The O3 run did not actually use the out-of-order CPU. Pass --cpu-type=O3CPU explicitly.

Exercise 11.2. Which tool would you use to confirm that a program's answer is correct, without caring about timing?

Answer

Spike, the golden RISC-V instruction-set simulator: fast, functional, no timing.

Exercise 11.3 (Ripes). Run the array-sum program on the five-stage processor without forwarding and note the cycle count. Repeat with forwarding and hazard detection. Then move addi a0,a0,4 between the load and its use and run again. Screenshot one load-use bubble and one flush after a taken branch, and annotate them.

Answer

The register a2 holds \(3+1+4+1+5+9+2+6 = 31\) every time. The cycle counts should satisfy: no forwarding > forwarding > forwarding with the reordered code. In the reordered version each lw is followed by an independent instruction, so the load-use bubble disappears; the taken-branch flush remains.

Exercise 11.4 (gem5). Write a C program that sums a large array (for example 4 MB) several times, and compile it statically for RISC-V. On O3CPU, sweep --l2_size over 64kB, 256kB, 1MB and 4MB, recording the IPC and the L2 miss rate. At one size, compare TimingSimpleCPU with O3CPU. Plot IPC against L2 size. Where does it flatten, and why there?

Answer

IPC rises and the L2 miss rate falls as the cache grows, sharply once the array fits in the L2 cache and then flattening (diminishing returns). TimingSimple's IPC can never exceed 1; O3 should be clearly higher on the same binary. Exact numbers depend on your gem5 version, so report it.

Exercise 11.5. Use the hand model of Example 11.1 to predict the loop cycle count, with forwarding, for an array of 16 words instead of 8. What is the CPI?

Answer

There are 16 passes of 5 instructions: 80 instructions. The first 15 passes each take \(5 + 1 + 2 = 8\) cycles and the last takes \(5 + 1 = 6\): \(15 \times 8 + 6 = 126\) cycles. CPI \(= 126/80 = 1.575\). With the load-use bubble scheduled away: \(15 \times 7 + 5 = 110\) cycles, CPI \(= 1.375\).

Exercise 11.6. In the Verilator lab, why does a waveform file that is empty point to a missing switch rather than a bug in PicoRV32?

Answer

Verilator records nothing unless tracing is enabled both at build time (the --trace option) and in the harness (traceEverOn(true) and the dump calls). An empty file therefore means that tracing was never switched on, not that the core misbehaved.

Exercise 11.7 (design study). Pick option A, B, C or D of Section 11.7, state a hypothesis with a predicted size of effect, and describe exactly what you will run for the baseline and the variant, how many repetitions you will use, and what result would make you reject your hypothesis.

Answer

There is no single answer; a good one has a measurable prediction ("a stride prefetcher will raise the IPC of a sequential array sum by more than 10%"), a baseline and a variant that differ in exactly one parameter, at least three runs of each with the median and spread reported, a stated tool version and flags, and a rejection criterion ("if the IPC changes by less than the run-to-run spread, I conclude the prefetcher does not help this program"). A reader should be able to repeat the experiment from the report alone.

docs.title: Chapter 6: On-Chip Interconnect
docs.text:
A modern system-on-chip is a city of dozens of blocks: CPU clusters, DMA engines, memory controllers, accelerators and a swarm of peripherals, all of which must reach memory and each other. The interconnect is the road network that lets them share access without gridlock. This chapter builds up from the golden rule of on-chip protocols, the VALID/READY handshake, through the AMBA family (APB, AHB and AXI), TileLink, Wishbone and CHI, to full networks-on-chip, and ends with two small models that show where the performance of a bus really comes from.

You need the idea of a memory-mapped address from Chapters 1 and 4 and the notion of coherence from Chapter 5 for the remarks on TileLink and CHI.

docs.title: 6.1 Why a chip needs roads
docs.text: A single core wired directly to a single memory needs no interconnect. A real chip has many blocks that start transactions and many that answer them, and wiring each directly to every other would need about \(n^2/2\) connections for \(n\) blocks, which would cover the die. Instead the blocks attach to a shared fabric that routes, arbitrates and decodes on their behalf. A city does not build a private road from every house to every shop; it builds a road network with junctions and traffic lights.

docs.title: Who asks, and who answers
docs.text: A manager starts transactions: "read address A", "write this to B". CPU cores, GPUs and DMA engines (hardware that copies blocks of data by itself) are managers. Older documents say master. A subordinate responds: a memory, a block of control registers, a FIFO, a serial port. Older documents say slave. One block can be both: a DMA engine moves data as a manager, but its settings are written by the CPU, so to the CPU it is a subordinate.

docs.title: Every subordinate owns an address range
